What Stocks Have Done Under a Republican President and a Democratic Congress
sum: Tuesday’s midterms were one for the history books. Democrats won control of both the House and Senate, and they picked up governorships in Ohio, Texas and Georgia. Kansas elected a Democrat to the Senate for the first time since 1932. Our home state of Texas did so for the first time in 38 years.

Voters were clearly focused on their wallets. Heading into the election, diesel averaged $6.34 a gallon, gasoline $4.23 and 30-year mortgage rates about 7.4%, according to CLSA. Even Vice President JD Vance said the war with Iran was the main reason Republicans lost.

Government policy is a precursor to change, so I asked my research team to dig into what the new lineup in Washington could mean for investors. When Congress is sworn in on January 3, a Republican president will face a Democratic House and Senate for the first time since George W. Bush’s final two years in office.

Midterm years have historically been the toughest stretch of the four-year presidential cycle. Since 1944, the S&P 500 has averaged a gain of just 3.8% in midterm years, compared with 10.9% in the other three years, according to JPMorgan. Midterm years have also seen the deepest average drawdowns, at 18%.

This year has bucked the trend, with the S&P 500 up about 9.3% through October. And what comes after has historically been even better. The market has posted positive returns in the six and 12 months following every midterm since 1950. Deutsche Bank adds that the fourth quarter of a midterm year has been positive in 21 of the last 23 cycles, with an average gain of 7%.
Wall Street likes to say that political gridlock is good for stocks. The data says it depends on who holds which branch.

Since 1950, the S&P 500 has averaged a 16.1% annual price gain when a Democratic president faced a Republican Congress, and 17.6% when a Democratic president faced a split Congress. The composition we’re about to get—a Republican president and Democratic Congress—has averaged just 4.8%, the lowest of the six combinations, according to Bloomberg data.

sum: As concerns over the profitability of AI shook tech and semiconductor stocks, ETFs (exchange-traded funds) investing in global major pharmaceutical companies are emerging. In particular, expectations are growing as the performance of obesity treatment development companies has grown significantly.

According to KOSCOM ETF Check on the 3rd, as of that day, the one-month return rate (based on reinvestment of distributions) of 'RISE Global Obesity Industry TOP2+' was 14.24%, ranking second in returns among all ETFs (excluding leverage and inverse).

Kim Min-su, team leader of the Global ETF Management Team at Mirae Asset Asset Management, explained, "This is due to the expansion of sales by leading obesity treatment companies being confirmed in performance, and continued expectations for next-generation treatment development."

Eli Lilly, which developed the obesity treatment 'Mounjaro,' had third-quarter revenue of $24.4 billion (approximately 32.6862 trillion won), a 38.6% increase year-on-year. EPS (earnings per share) was $7.48, up 6.6%. Revenue exceeded market consensus estimates by 1.1%, and EPS by 31.7%.

sum: The end of an earnings season can be a great time to discover new stocks and assess how companies are handling the current business environment. Let's take a look at how S&P Global (NYSE:SPGI) and the rest of the financial exchanges & data stocks fared in Q2.

Financial exchanges and data providers operate trading platforms and sell market information. They enjoy relatively stable revenue from trading fees and subscriptions, increasing demand for data analytics, and expansion opportunities in emerging markets. Challenges include regulatory oversight of market structure, competition from alternative trading venues, and substantial technology investments needed to maintain low-latency trading infrastructure and data security.
The 10 financial exchanges & data stocks we track reported a satisfactory Q2. As a group, revenues beat analysts' consensus estimates by 1.6%.
Thankfully, share prices of the companies have been resilient as they are up 9% on average since the latest earnings results.

Tracing its roots back to 1860 when it published the first railroad industry manual, S&P Global (NYSE:SPGI) provides credit ratings, market intelligence, commodity data, automotive analytics, and financial indices that help investors and businesses make decisions.

sum: A number of stocks jumped in the afternoon session after Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller signaled support for holding interest rates steady amid emerging signs of disinflation. During a Reuters NEXT Newsmaker interview, Governor Waller stated that if the positive economic trends seen over the last few months continue in the data due over the next two weeks, he would be inclined to support holding the federal funds target rate at its current setting. Waller pointed out that the three-month annualized inflation rate as measured by the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index has dropped from 4.76% in February to 3.05% currently, representing an encouraging downward trajectory.However, Waller warned that considerable uncertainty remains regarding how global conflicts, trade policy, and artificial intelligence will affect prices, according to Bloomberg. He cautioned that if upcoming August data shows this disinflationary progress has been fleeting, a rate hike may still be appropriate when the FOMC meets on September 15 and 16. Following Waller's comments, market-implied odds for a September rate hike dropped to 48.4%, down 15 percentage points from the prior day, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge cited by CNBC.

items.t: S&P Global Inc Stock (SPGI) Closed Down by 3.95% on Jul 21: Drivers Behind the Movement
sum: S&P Global Inc (SPGI) closed down by 3.95%. The Industrial & Commercial Services sector is down by 0.54%. The company underperformed the industry. Top 3 stocks by turnover in the sector: Nebius Group NV (NBIS) up 18.94%; Equifax Inc (EFX) down 4.38%; MSCI Inc (MSCI) down 10.36%.

The recent downward movement in S&P Global’s shares is primarily driven by a shift in macroeconomic expectations regarding the trajectory of interest rates and their subsequent impact on the debt capital markets. As a dominant leader in the credit ratings industry, the company’s financial performance is intrinsically linked to global debt issuance volumes. Recent data indicating persistent inflationary pressures has fueled speculation that the Federal Reserve may maintain a restrictive monetary policy for longer than the market had initially priced in. This hawkish outlook has pushed benchmark treasury yields higher, creating a direct headwind for corporate borrowing and refinancing activities, which are the primary engines for the company’s Ratings segment.

Beyond the immediate macro environment, the broader financial services sector is grappling with a period of heightened risk aversion. Institutional investors appear to be recalibrating their exposure to companies with high valuation multiples that are sensitive to capital market cycles. While S&P Global’s Market Intelligence and Indices divisions provide a robust cushion of recurring subscription revenue, these segments are not entirely insulated from a general tightening of corporate budgets. If global financial institutions anticipate a period of lower trading volumes or reduced asset under management growth, the demand for premium data and indexing services could face a temporary plateau, prompting a reassessment of the stock’s short-term growth trajectory.

Sentiment has been further dampened by cautious commentary from across the financial data and analytics industry. When major players in the credit assessment space signal a slowdown in deal flow or a more challenging environment for new bond coupons, it often triggers a broad sell-off across the peer group. This collective industry move suggests that the current decline is less about idiosyncratic operational issues and more about a systemic reaction to a tightening credit cycle.

Oracle Shares Fall 4% to One-Year Low: S&P Downgrades Credit Rating to BBB-, OpenAI Named as Risk
sum: On July 20, Eastern Time, Oracle shares dropped to a multi-month low following an S&P Global credit downgrade to BBB-. The downgrade reflects significant risks stemming from extreme customer concentration, as OpenAI represents nearly half of Oracle’s $638 billion backlog. Analysts express concern over deepening free cash flow deficits, projected to hit negative $42 billion by fiscal year 2027 due to massive data center capital expenditures. Market sentiment currently favors asset-light peers, penalizing Oracle’s capital-intensive, high-debt business model. If key clients face setbacks, Oracle’s balance sheet remains vulnerable to substantial idle capacity and rising maintenance costs.
TradingKey - On July 20, Eastern Time, Oracle ( ORCL) saw its shares fall as much as 4% to a new low since April 2025. As of press time, the stock was down 2.94% at $122.69.

It is reported that S&P Global recently downgraded its credit rating to BBB-, just one notch away from junk status. Although the stock rebounded from its intraday low, market debate over this legacy tech giant continues.

Just two weeks ago, S&P Global downgraded Oracle's credit rating to 'BBB-', leaving it just one step away from 'junk' status. The rating agency cited extreme customer concentration risk: OpenAI alone accounts for about half of Oracle's approximately $638 billion backlog of remaining performance obligations (RPO). However, OpenAI is currently facing headwinds from China's new AI model, Kimi K3, as well as pressure from a lawsuit by Apple.

Meanwhile, S&P expects its free cash flow deficit to continue to widen. Dragged down by the massive buildout of AI data centers, Oracle's free cash flow deficit is projected to reach a negative $42 billion in fiscal year 2027.

S&P's downgrade logic is clear: if OpenAI runs into trouble or even collapses, a massive amount of the data center capacity Oracle built for it will sit idle. Operations, maintenance, and depreciation expenses will continue to be incurred as usual, but with no corresponding customer revenue to cover them—leaving the balance sheet to bear the brunt.
In sharp contrast to Oracle's stock price hitting a one-year low, its peers have risen, with asset-light Cloudflare ( NET) and Snowflake ( SNOW) rising 40.33% and 25.66% respectively this year.

The Real Engine Behind S&P Global Stock Is Not What You Think
sum: While investors fixate on the company’s famous Ratings business, its high-margin Indices division is delivering a powerful and timely boost.

With S&P Global (SPGI) stock -21.2% over the past year, it’s easy to see why investors are cautious. The headlines are dominated by geopolitical conflict and macroeconomic uncertainty, factors that can chill the debt issuance markets that feed the company’s well-known Ratings division. The stock’s performance suggests the market has priced in plenty of concern about this core business.

But underneath the noise, a different part of the company is telling a much stronger story. The number to watch is the 17% year-over-year revenue growth from its S&P Dow Jones Indices division. That figure, from the most recent quarter, shows a powerful business hitting its stride, with double-digit growth across all its business lines.

This is far more than another revenue stream. The Indices business is a profitability machine. It posted a 73.8% operating margin in the first quarter, meaning its growth has an outsized impact on the company’s bottom line. When this segment accelerates, it provides a significant lift to overall earnings power, something a simple look at the headline revenue might miss.

The growth is also broad-based. Revenue from asset-linked fees, tied to the value of funds that track its indexes, grew 18%. And, crucially, revenue from exchange-traded derivatives also jumped 18%. That second piece is the key to understanding this segment’s unique strength right now.

The very market volatility that creates headwinds for the Ratings business can act as a tailwind for the Indices division. Management calls this a “natural hedge we have in this business during times of geopolitical and macroeconomic disruptions.” When uncertainty rises, trading activity in derivatives linked to indices often increases, driving revenue for S&P Global.

This provides a powerful counterbalance inside the company. While skeptics rightly focus on how market jitters could slow debt issuance, they may be overlooking how those same jitters are fueling a highly profitable, parallel engine. The recent results show this is no mere theory; it’s happening now.
